heading.en: How a monopolist sets output and price

hook.en: The only cable operator in a town can charge any price, but if it charges too much, few homes subscribe. Where does it stop?

objectives.en: Derive MR from a straight-line AR curve
Find monopoly equilibrium using MR = MC

narration.en: The only cable operator in a town can charge any price, but if it charges too much, few homes subscribe. Where does it stop?

body.en: Since the monopolist must lower the price to sell more, its AR (demand) curve slopes down and MR lies below AR. For a straight-line demand P = a − bQ, TR = aQ − bQ² and MR = a − 2bQ: the MR line starts at the same point on the price axis and is twice as steep. MR is zero where TR is at its maximum, at the mid-point of the AR line.

points.en: AR = price, falls as output rises
MR < AR at every output after the first
Linear AR: MR is twice as steep

text.en: Competitive output would be where P = MC: Q = 40.

body.en: A monopolist maximises profit where MR = MC and MC is rising or cuts MR from below. The price is read off the AR curve at that output. If AR > AC there is supernormal profit, which can last in the long run because entry is blocked. Compared with perfect competition, a monopoly produces less and charges more, since its price is above MC. The monopolist always produces on the elastic part of its demand curve, because MR is positive there.

points.en: Conditions: MR = MC, and MC cuts MR from below
Supernormal profit can persist in the long run
Less output and a higher price than perfect competition

prompt.en: Arrange the steps to find a monopolist's equilibrium price and profit.

steps.en: Write the demand (AR) function and find TR = P × Q
Differentiate or difference TR to get MR
Set MR equal to MC and solve for output
Read the price from the AR curve at that output
Find profit = TR − TC (or (AR − AC) × Q)
